📊 1. Task 5: Truth Table Complexity & Exponential Cliff

Task 5 evaluates a propositional logic formula bottom-up on its parse tree across all possible truth assignments. For a formula containing k distinct atoms, the truth assignment space consists of exactly 2k rows.

Figure 1: Truth Table execution time vs. number of atoms k (Left: Linear scale, Right: Logarithmic scale showing exact O(2^k) slope).

The Exponential Explosion (Why 20 Atoms is the Limit)

The empirical results cleanly validate the theoretical time complexity of O(2k · N):

Atoms (k) Total Rows (2k) Runtime (μs) Runtime (ms) Unit Cost per Row
k = 2 4 0.16 μs 0.000 ms 38.95 ns
k = 4 16 1.80 μs 0.002 ms 112.23 ns
k = 6 64 13.92 μs 0.014 ms 217.50 ns
k = 8 256 88.47 μs 0.088 ms 345.59 ns
k = 10 1,024 509.12 μs 0.509 ms 497.19 ns
k = 12 4,096 3,081.34 μs 3.081 ms 752.28 ns
k = 14 16,384 17,937.76 μs 17.938 ms 1094.83 ns
k = 16 65,536 89,857.01 μs 89.857 ms 1371.11 ns
k = 18 262,144 389,619.19 μs 389.619 ms 1486.28 ns
k = 20 1,048,576 1,740,759.98 μs 1,740.760 ms 1660.12 ns
Figure 2: Amortized cost per evaluated row (nanoseconds) as atom count k increases.
Key Empirical Finding: Across actual runs, the unit evaluation cost per row scaled from 38.95 ns/row at k=2 to 1660.12 ns/row at k=20 (with total execution time for 1,048,576 rows reaching 1.74 seconds). This occurs because each leaf evaluation performs a linear lookup in AtomTable (costing O(k) per atom). Consequently, row evaluation time scales as O(k · N), perfectly matching empirical measurements.

🔄 2. Task 3: Parse Tree Traversals (Recursive vs. Iterative)

Task 3 requires implementing In-Order, Pre-Order, and Post-Order traversals both recursively and iteratively. All six traversals visit every node in the tree exactly once, yielding theoretical time complexity O(N).

Empirical Traversal Findings:
  • In-Order & Pre-Order: Recursive and Iterative implementations exhibit near-parity (measured mean ratio 1.02x). Modern C compilers (GCC -O3) optimize recursive tail and non-tail frames into efficient register jumps.
  • Post-Order: The iterative two-stack algorithm incurs higher overhead (measured mean ratio 1.36x) because every node must be pushed onto Stack 1 and then popped and pushed onto Stack 2. In contrast, recursive post-order traverses the call-stack natively with zero secondary allocation.

🌲 3. Task 4: Tree Height & Structural Bounds

The height of a parse tree is defined as the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. For any binary parse tree with N nodes, the tree height h is strictly bounded:
⌈log2(N + 1)⌉ - 1 ≤ h ≤ N - 1

Figure 5: Measured tree height vs. theoretical bounds for balanced vs. degenerate (skewed) parse trees.
Figure 6: Height computation runtime: Recursive (post-order DFS) vs. Iterative (BFS Queue).
Algorithmic Difference in Task 4:
  • Recursive Height: Uses post-order depth-first traversal: h = 1 + max(left, right). Space on the call stack is O(h).
  • Iterative Height: Uses level-order breadth-first traversal via a FIFO queue tracking depth. Space in the queue reaches O(W) where W is maximum tree width (up to N/2 leaves in balanced trees).

💾 5. Memory Footprint & Stack Safety Analysis

Memory consumption comprises three distinct regions:

  1. Heap Memory (Parse Tree): Each node occupies 48 bytes (32 bytes label buffer + two 8-byte child pointers). Total heap footprint = N × 48 bytes.
  2. Call Stack Memory (Recursion): Each recursive call pushes an activation record (approx. 64 bytes on x86_64). Maximum call stack depth = h × 64 bytes. For balanced formulas h = O(log N) (under 2 KB); for degenerate skewed formulas h = O(N).
  3. Explicit Stack Memory (Iteration): Iterative algorithms allocate explicit pointer arrays (8 bytes per entry) in the heap/BSS segment, eliminating any risk of OS stack overflow on deep trees.
Figure 8: Memory allocation profile across Heap Nodes, Worst-Case Call Stack, and Iterative Buffer.

🎯 6. SAT 2002 Benchmark Suite Empirical Analysis

The SAT 2002 Competition benchmark suite consists of 1,964 instances divided into uniform generated benchmarks and submitted industrial/combinatorial problems.

Figure 9: Distribution of variable counts and clause-to-variable ratio (r = m/n) across benchmark suites.
Connection to Theoretical Logic: Notice the concentration of uniform benchmarks around clause-to-variable ratio r ≈ 4.26. In computational logic, random 3-SAT problems exhibit a sharp satisfiability phase transition at r ≈ 4.26, where the probability of satisfiability drops sharply from 1 to 0 and computational complexity peaks.

⚖️ 7. Algorithm Trade-Offs & Decision Matrix

A multi-dimensional evaluation of recursive vs. iterative paradigms across the five assignment tasks:

Metric Recursive Approaches Iterative Approaches Recommendation / Conclusion
Time Complexity O(N) O(N) Identical asymptotic behavior; recursive has slightly lower constant factor due to compiler register allocation.
Stack Safety Vulnerable to deep trees (O(N) stack frames) 100% Safe (uses heap-managed buffers) Iterative is mandatory in production parsers with uncontrolled recursion depth.
Code Complexity Clean & Concise (3-5 lines per traversal) Moderate (requires manual stack & queue loops) Recursive is ideal for academic demonstrations and bounded formulas.
Truth Table Scalability Hard Bound at k ≤ 20 Truth table evaluation is inherently exponential O(2k); SAT solvers (DPLL/CDCL) must be used for k > 25.
